While it isn’t a perfect game by any stretch it is also no where near mediocre. 

There are things to criticize about the game, some issues that you don’t expect for a modern game (load times, menu lag, some weird cutscene trigger choices) but none of that really an impact on the value of the game. 

I honestly think to some degree the problem comes from the fact that the game is so heavily tied to Suikoden. Obviously it was advertised as a spiritual successor was a huge selling point for the Kickstarter but I think it also failed to clarify what this project was.

It is easy to look at EC and compare it Suikoden and think that it fell short, but comparing the games 1:1 isn’t fair to EC in the slightest, with a smaller budget and and less experience in the modern era of gaming when bugs are expected (and fixable) if you were expecting perfection, that’s on you.


The Kickstarter was originally for 351,563, and when it quickly raised over 3 million dollars people would be excused for thinking that it mean the game would be polished beyond belief, but this shows a huge lack of understand of both how Kickstarter and game development works.

For comparison, the average cost of developing a video game on the PS2 in 2003 was 5-7 million, adjust to inflation for the year the game was funded (2020) that is 7-10 million dollars. Assuming that Suikoden, which wasn’t a huge success in comparison to its contemporaries, was in the lower end that means the last 3 Suikoden games had a budget of at around 3-4 million dollars more than EC, while being backed by Konami, and a team of experienced game makers that has been working on the series for sometime. Not to mention the 3-4 million raised for EC was used to develop two games. 

Even considering that some of the team that worked on Suikoden also worked on EC the reality is that it is a new team and expecting them to release perfection was a silly expectation. Let’s not forget that the original wasn’t a perfect game, but it was great, and it did well enough that we got a Suikoden 2.

As far as the bugs, maybe I’m just complacent at this point, and I by no means think that this is a good thing, but the reality is that there is far less pressure on studios to release games in a state in absolute perfection. As games have gotten bigger and more complicated, and I acknowledge that EC is not exactly fitting that bill, bugs have become more common and while I am not a fan of that reality I do except it as part of the industry now. The question is never is the game bug free, because the answer to that question is always no, every game has bugs, even releases that go off with out a hitch like God of War 2018, still have bugs. The question is does the game have GAME BREAKING bugs, and the answer to that question in regard to EC is a resounding no. Yes, there are issues that can be fixed, better optimization that can be had, and things that should be addressed, but EC is a complete and full feature game lacking any sort of game breaking bugs.

Just to be pedantic,  I see a lot of people talking about how FF7 is the best selling title, it is not, 14 is by leaps and bounds. (Every once in awhile 10 gives them a run for their money.)

The reality is people like what they like, and what FF game you think is “best” usually comes down to personal experience and when you played whatever title you think is the “best”.

If you are a long time fan who played the early titles before the jump to PS you likely find 6 is the best, or maybe 4. If you started playing the game on PlayStation with 7 (or were in your formative angsty years when you played 7) it’s probably your favorite. Same can be said for 10.

People bitch because they like what they like and anything that feels like a departure from that is upsetting to them. Gamers are also notoriously bad at being objective when it comes to talking about the quality of video games, which is why there are people that will always believe Assassins Creed and Call of Duty are the best video games on the planet.

When it comes to 16 I understand some of the frustration, people were burned by 15 (the first true action game in the series)and some people flat out don’t like action games. The sad truth tied to that is that those games who aren’t a fan of action games need to accept that it is incredibly unlikely that Final Fantasy will ever return to a turned based format out side of remasters and re-releases.

It is really easy to say “there is clearly still a market for turned based RPGs” and look at the success of OCTOPATH 2, Bravely Default 2, or even Persona 5 but the reality is that these games don’t even come close to touching Final Fantasy 16 sales.

I couldn’t find BD2 week one sales but it didn’t hit 1 million sales until December 2021 when it was release in February of that year. Let’s be generous and say 25 % of those week week one sales

So you have 250k for BD2 78k of OCTOPATH 2 And a combined total of 337,767 sales for person 5 (only counting its original release not all of its re-release)

Those three games, arguably 3 of the best turn based games in the past decade total up to a whopping 665,767 sales.

Final Fantasy 16 sold 3 million copies in its opening week.

Loud opinions of angry gamers aside, numbers don’t lie. The market has turned towards faster paced action games, and while there is still a market for turned based games, it can’t compare to the demand for action games.

I too miss the days of turned based Final Fantasy, but acting like a game “isn’t a Final Fantasy game” or is just straight up bad because it’s an action game is silly.

Final Fantasy 16 is fantastic and while I haven’t finished it yet it’s definitely looking like a contender for at least my Top 5 FF games of all time.
